problem: Video models give visual goals but not actions. Existing grounding needs an inverse-dynamics or goal-conditioned policy trained on embodiment-specific action-labeled demonstrations, or (AVDC) optical-flow/depth rigid-transform inference that is imprecise and unusable for deformable objects. Neither works well without action labels.
motivation: Action-labeled data is costly to collect and the learned policies generalize poorly out of distribution. Large video models encode rich task knowledge, so if they could be grounded to continuous actions through self-exploration alone, without rewards, action labels or masks, they would be much more usable for control.
key_idea: Use frames synthesized by a video model as visual goals for a goal-conditioned policy that explores online. Hindsight-relabel the rollouts into a replay buffer, and boost exploration with periodic random-action bootstrapping and action-chunk prediction.
insight: Both ingredients are needed. Without random-action bootstrapping (w/o rand) or without video guidance (w/o video), Libero success is 0.0 in both scenes, since the policy collapses to fixed actions or never finds task states. Action chunking beats single-action prediction (Scene 1: 42.2 vs 16.4; Scene 2: 62.0 vs 41.0). Extra periodic random exploration stabilizes training in Scene 1 (42.2 vs 28.0). Success saturates after about 200 video-guided rollouts, and the policy is robust to test-time video sampling rates.
method: Video-guided goal-conditioned exploration: a frozen video diffusion model f(x_start, c) generates frames; the policy pi(a|x_i, x_goal) is run with each generated frame as the goal in sequence, and the resulting image-action rollouts go into a replay buffer R.

Hindsight relabeling: the executed actions and observed images are treated as ground-truth dynamics, so even failed goal-reaching rollouts give valid training data (max log-likelihood of a_{i:i+h} given x_i, x_{i+h}; MSE/diffusion loss).

Periodic random action bootstrapping: uniform random-action episodes are added to R before training (warm-start 10k steps) and periodically afterwards (q_r=500), so the policy learns basic dynamics and avoids a self-reinforcing loop of degenerate actions.

Chunk-level action prediction and exploration: a CNN Diffusion Policy predicts a horizon-16 action chunk, executing 8, for coherent exploration. Random exploration uses chunks sampled around a uniformly sampled mean, Gaussian with length 24, to avoid zero-mean jitter.
Exploration grasping primitive (Libero): a simple heuristic that triggers a grasp when the gripper is close above an object, based on wrist-camera distance vs. gripper height.

Video model: AVDC-style lightweight 3D-UNet with CLIP text encoding, trained from scratch per environment on action-free demo image sequences (20 demos per task for Libero and iTHOR, 15 for Meta-World, where the AVDC checkpoint is used). Also a SuSIE image-editing subgoal variant.
Navigation variant: in iTHOR a ResNet18+MLP predicts a single discrete action (horizon 1); long-range navigation is done by re-generating video from the last observation.

setting.backbone: Video model: AVDC-style 3D-UNet diffusion + CLIP text encoder (trained from scratch, frozen during exploration); Policy: CNN Diffusion Policy with ResNet18 (manipulation), ResNet18+3-layer MLP (iTHOR), trained from scratch by self-exploration
setting.training_data: Action-free demonstration image sequences to train the video model only (Libero 20 demos/task = 160 total; Meta-World 15/task; iTHOR 20/task); the policy is trained on self-collected online rollouts plus random-action episodes, with no action labels, rewards or masks
setting.observation: monocular RGB image (128x128) of the current observation plus generated goal image; task language description for the video model
setting.action_space: continuous end-effector delta pose + gripper (7-D Libero/Calvin, 4-D Meta-World) as action chunks; discrete {Move Ahead, Turn Left, Turn Right, Done} in iTHOR
setting.privileged: none at test time (AVDC baseline is given target-object segmentation masks, the proposed method is not); simulator success checks are used to terminate rollouts and evaluate

numbers.eval_set_note: 4 scenes (Kitchen, Living Room, Bedroom, Bathroom) x 3 targets = 12 targets; random start positions
numbers.backbone: AVDC-style video model + ResNet18+MLP policy (trained by self-exploration)
numbers.extra: no action labels; video model trained on 20 image-only demos per task
numbers.evidence: Table 5 (Quantitative Results on iThor Navigation), Overall columns per scene for Ours

numbers_note: The paper's main results are manipulation success rates (Libero, Meta-World, Calvin); no canonical embodied navigation benchmark. iTHOR results are per-scene success rates; overall per-task numbers are in the tables. Manipulation overall SRs: Libero Scene1 42.2 (Ours) / 54.8 (Ours w/ SuSIE), Scene2 62.0 / 50.2; Meta-World 67.2; Calvin 84.4. Not encodable as canonical navigation benchmarks.
results: Without action labels, the method matches or surpasses BC baselines trained on expert actions: Libero overall 42.2/62.0 vs. best baseline Diffusion Policy BC 46.0/49.2, Meta-World 67.2 vs. 52.8 (GCBC), Calvin 84.4 vs. 68.8 (DP BC). In iTHOR navigation it is on par with BC/GCBC and beats AVDC by about 36% on average (e.g. Kitchen 48.3 vs. 12.2).
limitations: Random exploration struggles with tasks needing very precise manipulation (Meta-World assembly 16.8, Libero placement tolerances), and can cause unsafe contacts on real robots.
Requires dozens to hundreds of video-guided rollouts with environment resets, easy in simulation but hard in the real world; only evaluated in simulation.
Bounded by video model quality (hallucination, task/video mismatch, small video model trained from scratch per environment); the grasp exploration primitive is a heuristic.
